newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CLINTONS VISIT SAFRICA HOUSING PROJECT.
newsitem.headline: CLINTONS VISIT SAFRICA HOUSING PROJECT.

text.p: Ululations of joy greeted U.S. first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton on Wednesday as she and daughter Chelsea toured a dusty, windblown piece of land where homeless women were building concrete houses.
Shortly after arriving at Cape Town airport, on the second day of her three-day visit to South Africa, Mrs. Clinton stopped at the Victoria Mxenge homes project.

The development is one of many being undertaken in post-apartheid South Africa to try to get proper homes to an estimated one million people who live in poverty, many of them in dense "squatter towns".
Mrs. Clinton told the assembled women that they were working to "build not only houses but a great spirit about what can be accomplished when people work together to help themselves."

The visit to the project emphasised a key goal of her two-week tour of six countries in Africa -- promoting better rights and education for women and children. Of 268 people working at the site, 260 were women.

She was expected later to attend with South African Archbishop Desmond Tutu a meeting of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which offers amnesty to people who confess to political crimes carried out during the apartheid era in an attempt to lead to reconciliation.

Mrs. Clinton was led on a tour of the housing project by barefooted Patricia Matolengwe, leader of the South African Homeless People's Federation. A single mother who lives in a shack, she wore a traditional Xhosa costume of bright orange with streaks of white painted on her skin.

Women sang and chanted in the Xhosa tribal language and ululated as Mrs. Clinton toured the worksite, where homes were in various stages of construction. Some women pushed wheelbarrows while others mixed concrete.
She entered one house, a simple structure of gray concrete brick with modest furniture inside. On the wall was a ceramic moulding that said, "The family that prays together, stays together."
At a welcoming ceremony afterward, a breeze blew dust over Mrs. Clinton, daughter Chelsea and the crowd of 250 or so who gathered around to hear President Clinton's wife.
"I wanted to come and see for myself what I heard about the Federation's work because you are not only building houses, you are building your country," Mrs. Clinton told them.
She said she would tell President Clinton about it and that if invited back, "I might be able to bring my husband back as well."

The women presented Mrs. Clinton with a dark green iron kettle. As Metalongwe presented it to her, she said: "You have to cook something for your husband and we want to know if you cook." Mrs. Clinton smiled and laughed.
